Pitt stole the movie out from under DiCaprio's feet, however. The guy has got incredible charm and charisma. But chubby old DiCaprio, who isn't aging well, held his own in the important scenes.

Now some points of interest:

Tarantino's obsession with women's feet is becoming annoying and tedious. I got tired of looking at dirty female feet.

Was it a kind of counterpoint to the pedophilia of Roman Polanski? Polanski's pedo tendencies are nevere actually shown or even hinted at in the movie.

The narrator, who speaks over parts of the movie, was jarring and out of place, and completely unnecessary. Tarantino made a mistake by including a narrator.

The flamethrower used by DiCaprio was just plain stupid. I don't know what else to call it, but when DiCaprio's character brings it out to the pool in the final scenes, it made me cringe in embarrassment for him and for Tarantino. What a poor decision. Obviously it was Tarantino's attempt to top the sword at the end of Pulp Fiction but it didn't work at all.

I said the first two hours of this movie were good, because the last twenty minutes or so were terrible. For those who don't know, they involve the attack by the Manson Family on the Polanski residence ... except, this is a fairy tale, right? "Once Upon A Time" in Hollywood? So Tarantino decided to make Sharon Tate and Roman Polanski live happily ever after, by having the Manson Family attack the house next door to the Polanski residence. Pitt and DiCaprio, with the help of a very appealing pit bull, trash the Manson family members, preventing them from killing anyone.

I have to admit, the final scenes where DiCaprio walks up to the iron gate in the Polanski residence, after the battle with Squeakie Fromm and the other Manson Family members, and is asked to come into the house by a very pregnant Sharon Tate, were sort of touching. It is a "What could have been" kind of moment -- the way it might have been in an alternative universe if the attack by the Manson Family had failed. Tarantino directed it as a kind of love letter to Polanski and Tate, who was murdered by the Manson Family in 1969 along with her unborn baby.

But Tarantino's ending departs so radically from history, it's impossible to accept it. I found it very unsatisfying and deceptive. I felt as though Tarantino had deliberately cheated me. The ending spoils the entire movie, which otherwise would have been pretty good. The wild rides down the Hollywood Hills, shot from inside the cars, were great -- not as well directed as they might have been, but still a great concept as a way of conveying the freedom of the times. Over all, I was disappointed, but found the movie interesting. I'd say it is worth watching.
